A report by The Indian Express has highlighted the sharp rise in government-issued blocking orders to social media platforms between March and July, during the period of the CJP student protests.

Most of these directions were issued through the Sahyog portal, a government platform used by Central and state agencies to send blocking notices to social media companies. The report says many of these orders were issued under Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act, 2000, which requires intermediaries to remove unlawful content to retain their legal protection. These are separate from blocking directions issued under Section 69A of the IT Act.

The report also says Meta has integrated its API with Sahyog to comply with the government’s 2–3-hour deadline, potentially allowing content flagged through government directions to be blocked automatically without a separate human review.

Digital-rights advocates have raised concerns about this mechanism and its implications for due process and freedom of expression.

Statement on the Indian government's order to GitHub to block BitChat:

The Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (@Cyberdost ) under the Ministry of Home Affairs (@PIBHomeAffairs) has ordered GitHub (@github) to remove three URLs linking to BitChat, an app that works offline without an internet connection and enables users to communicate over Bluetooth. This order was issued under Section 79(3)(b) of the Information Technology Act, 2000, read with Rule 3(1)(d) of the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021.

During the internet shutdowns imposed on multiple occasions over the past week in parts of Central Delhi, many protesters faced difficulties communicating or seeking emergency services. Open-source applications like BitChat allow people to communicate with other people using the same application nearby, without an internet connection.

The order states that the application would impede the state's ability to conduct lawful interception and surveillance and enable users to circumvent lawful restrictions such as internet shutdowns. The notice was issued at 11:16 PM on 23rd July and has given GitHub three hours to remove the links.

However, the order fails to satisfy the tests of legality, necessity, and proportionality and constitutes as an abject misuse of Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act, read with Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules 2021.

At the outset, Section 79(3)(b) does not confer the power to block or remove content, which instead stems from Section 69A of the IT Act. The issuance of orders with generic grounds is further inconsistent with the safeguards laid down by the Supreme Court in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India. The Supreme Court upheld Section 69A of the IT Act, 2000 strictly because it required that blocking orders must be reasoned, necessary, and proportionate, and that such reasons must be recorded in writing to enable judicial review.

The opacity surrounding these removals goes against the strict requirements of accountability and record-keeping embedded in the Information Technology (Procedure and Safeguards for Blocking for Access of Information by Public) Rules, 2009.

The only reason this particular order in the current instance became public is not due to dissemination by the issuing authority, but rather because @Jack posted about the same on X. What we see emerging through these removals is a system of informal, decentralised censorship, where the government can direct content removals without transparency or oversight.

The lack of information renders a meaningful legal challenge impossible and leaves affected parties without legal redressal, including the basic elements of review that Section 69A provides when read with the Blocking Rules 2009. Orders passed under Section 79(3)(b) therefore function as circumventions of the procedural safeguards enumerated under Section 69A of the IT Act.

text:
Statement : Shutting down Telegram is a band aid solution and is a disproportionate answer to exam fraud

The Internet Freedom Foundation objects to the directions announced today in the National Testing Agency's press release on action against the Telegram platform. On the NTA's recommendation, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology has, under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, restricted access to the whole of Telegram in India until 22 June 2026, and has separately ordered the platform to switch off message-editing for every Indian user until 30 June 2026. This is a blunt, nationwide measure aimed at the conduct of rampant fraud rackets, and on the Government's own admission is constitutionally incompatible.

At the outset it is important to note that Section 69A and the Blocking Rules of 2009 framed under it allow the Government to block access to specific “information” on a computer resource. They do not extend to switching off an entire intermediary, still less to ordering a company to redesign its product by removing a feature for a whole country. In Shreya Singhal v Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A because it is narrow and hedged with procedural safeguards. Reading it to authorise shutting down a platform that lakhs use is an overbroad restriction by the NTAs own admission. For the message-editing direction the release identifies no source of power at all. If one exists, the order must say so.

The release argues against itself

A restriction on access has to be the least intrusive measure that achieves its aim as per the constitutional test of proportionality laid down in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) and applied in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020). The NTA's own narration shows the block fails its nodal agency, the release says, “has secured the prompt take-down of a substantial number of Telegram channels, groups and bots”, and this targeted work “is the reason the harm caused by these rackets has been contained to the extent it has”. If channel level takedown contained the harm, the case for a blanket block collapses and hence the Government has reached for a heavier tool while conceding that a lighter one was working. The collateral cost sits on the record too as noted in the press release. The block, the NTA accepts, “affects lakhs of citizens who use the Telegram platform for legitimate personal, educational, professional and informational purposes”. The release also says there is "no such paper available outside the secured examination chain" and that “the security of the examination is unaffected by the action taken”. If the exam is secure and no leak exists, what is being suppressed is rumour, and rumour cannot justify closing a platform when specific blocking and criminal prosecution remain available.

Students use of Telegram

The block of telegram is reactive and ineffective and will punish ordinary users instead of addressing the systemic source of exam leaks. This blocking comes in the final days of NEET preparation, when thousands of students depend on Telegram for study groups, doubt-clearing, and shared resources. Also, it is important to consider that the source of exam papers leak will occur from inside the system, among insiders and across the printing and logistics chain, with the platform being the most downstream channel for distribution. Hence, switching off Telegram, is merely a deflection from the repeated failures that will continue while media attention is directed towards this Telegram ban.

Lack of transparency

At present only a press release from the NTA has been provided, which recommended the block but the reasoned order of MeitY, the authority that issued it, has not been released. The Anuradha Bhasin decision requires that orders restricting access be published so they can be tested in court. Here the order, and the reasoning of the committee behind it, stay out of view, and we do not know whether Telegram was heard at all. An announcement of a block is no substitute for an order the affected party can challenge.
Blunt to enforce and very easy to evade
Usually, app-level blocks run through IS-level DNS and IP filtering. They are over inclusive, sweeping in lawful use, yet simple to evade as a determined exam leak racket moves to a VPN or a mirror within minutes while ordinary users lose the service for a week.

We ask the Government to:

1) Publish the MeitY Section 69A order and the NTA recommendation behind it, with reasons;
2) State the legal basis for the message editing direction, or withdraw it;
3) Confirm whether Telegram was given a hearing under the Blocking Rules, and place the committee's record before any court that hears a challenge; and
4) Lift the platform-wide restriction and rely on the targeted takedowns the NTA itself credits with containing the harm.

We emphasise that the NEET (UG) 2026 re-examination is worth protecting and it concerns the future of lakhs of aspirants. It requires securing the entire process of examination rather than reaching for purported band aid solutions that instead cause more harm. The State cannot switch off a service used by lakhs to answer the wrongdoing of a few, and cannot do it through an order no one affected is allowed to read. On its own facts, the Government has done both.

New Delhi, 16 June 2026.

IFF Statement: Blocking of the Cockroach Janta Party's Instagram account

July 22, 2026

The Instagram account of the Cockroach Janta Party (@cockroachjantaparty) is no longer accessible to users in India. Meta's notice states only that it complied with "a legal request to restrict this content". No order has been published and the legal basis, the issuing authority, and the reasons remain unknown.

We emphasise that the account is primarily engaged in acts of political speech that enjoy the full protection of Article 19(1)(a). The account has been restricted after the movement's march to Parliament over the NEET paper leak, and while the Delhi High Court examines allegations of excessive police force against protesters. Viewed in this background the blocking of its social media account at this moment is the suppression of dissent.

The secrecy compounds the illegality. In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A of the IT Act on the strength of its procedural safeguards. In Anuradha Bhasin, it held that orders restricting fundamental rights must be published. These safeguards are defeated when the originator learns of a blocking action from an error message.

We also note that Meta's notice refers to a "legal request", not an order.  We call on MeitY to disclose the order, furnish a copy to the account holder, and provide a hearing. We call on Meta to inform the account holder of the specific legal process it received. Wholesale blocking of an entire account is disproportionate and unconstitutional.

Sound the Alarm : IFF’s First Read on MeitY's Draft IT Rules Second Amendment, 2026

New Delhi, 30 March 2026

On 30 March 2026, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology published proposed amendments to the IT Rules, 2021, inviting public comments by 14 April,  a comment period of barely fifteen days for changes with far reaching consequences for free speech and intermediary governance in India. We have conducted a quick review of the draft amendments. Despite being presented as "clarificatory and procedural," they represent a dangerous expansion of executive power over online speech.

We wish to state at the outset that these proposed amendments need to be immediately withdrawn and every member in our citizenry should demand their roll back and stand with the Constitution of India. These proposed amendments come at a time of fear and increased government directed censorship, especially of online political speech that includes parody and satire of the government, including the Prime Minister.

In brief the five changes are listed below:

1. Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h): Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law.

2. Rule 3(4): Insertion of a new clause that mandates intermediary compliance with MeitY-issued clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines, making such compliance a condition for retaining safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act. These are not anchored to the rule making powers of the IT Act, 2000 and provide uncanalised power to MEITY despite it stating otherwise.

3. Rule 8(1) proviso: A substitution in the proviso that expands applicability of MIB’s oversight mechanism in Part III of the rules to:  (1) intermediaries and (2) users who are not “publishers” and post/share news and current affairs content online. This oversight mechanism contains the blocking powers of MIB by way of Rule 14 (Inter-Departmental Committee), Rule 15 (Procedure for issuing directions to block), and Rule 16 (Emergency blocking provisions).

4. Rule 14(2) : A substitution that expands the scope of the IDC from hearing "complaints or grievances" to hearing "matters", including those referred by the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting.

5. Rule 14(5) : Replaces "complaints or grievances" with "the matter" in relation to IDC examination and recommendations.

A massive expansion of an unconstitutional censorship and regulatory power

First and most concerningly, Rule 3(4) creates a sweeping power for MeitY to issue binding instruments which are not anchored in law such as clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines that intermediaries must comply with as a condition of safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act.

The Supreme Court's 2015 judgment in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, remains the foundational precedent governing intermediary liability. It constrains the proposed amendments in several ways. First, the court read down Section 79(3)(b) to require that "actual knowledge" of unlawful content must come through a court order or government notification. Any Rule 3(4) making MeitY, "clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs", lower the constitutional threshold for intermediary due diligence obligations.

Further, the settled principle in Indian administrative law, reaffirmed in Indian Express Newspapers v. Union of India (1985) 1 SCC 641 and Confederation of Ex-Servicemen Associations v. Union of India (2006) 8 SCC 399, is that delegated legislation must remain within the four corners of the parent statute.  It is important to note that the rule-making power under Section 87(1) of the IT Act is confined to, "carry[ing] out the provisions" of the Act. Section 87(2)(zg) authorizes rules for intermediary guidelines under Section 79(2), and Section 87(2)(z) for blocking procedures under Section 69A(2). Justice Chandurkar's judgement in the Kunal Kamra case clearly found the FCU amendment was not properly referable to either provision. Hence, any Rule 3(4) mandating compliance with MeitY advisories would face identical challenges since they create substantive new obligations not contemplated by Sections 79 or 87.

Even though Rule 3(4)(b)(ii) states that such, “advisories” etc. need to, “clearly specify the statutory provision or legal basis under which it is issued”, since these are not required to be published or made public there is every likelihood these will be issued with secrecy and hence may just in a tautological manner refer back to Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act. This is similar to a logical fallacy in which it is clearly observable that a student is cheating on an exam who then claims that they may be permitted to continue cheating since they are stating at the same time they are not cheating. 

The practical effect of Rule 3(4) is that intermediaries face a perpetual compliance threat. Any failure to comply with any MeitY-issued instrument, however vague, however rapidly issued may cost them their safe harbour. The response for an intermediary is over-compliance and over-censorship.

Circumventing existing stay orders

The original proviso to Rule 8(1) stated that Part III applied to intermediaries only "for the purposes of rules 15 and 16"  i.e., content blocking directions and emergency blocking. The amended proviso now extends this to Rule 14, bringing intermediaries and user-generated news/current affairs content under the jurisdiction of the Inter-Departmental Committee.

Under Rules 9(1) and 9(3) of the 2021 IT Rules, there is a Code of Ethics compliance requirement and the three-tier grievance redressal mechanism, both of which were stayed by the Bombay High Court on 14 August 2021 as prima facie violative of Article 19(1)(a) and ultra vires the IT Act. On the oversight mechanism in Rules 14, 15, and 16, the Bombay High Court granted the petitioners to seek relief on this rule when an Inter Departmental Committee is established. The Madras High Court affirmed this stay as having pan-India effect in its order of 16 September 2021 in T.M. Krishna v. Union of India, observing that "an oversight mechanism to control the media by the government may rob the media of its independence." 

Both these cases, along with other cases challenging various provisions of the 2021 IT Rules, are now pending adjudication before the Delhi High Court.

The expansion of Rule 8(1) to cover Rules 14, 15, and 16 is an attempt to expand the blocking powers of MIB to both intermediaries and users who are not “publishers” but post news and current affairs content online. The IDC can now examine "matters" relating to user-generated news content on intermediary platforms without the Code of Ethics framework having been adjudicated as constitutional; the government effectively obtains the content oversight machinery that three High Courts found illegal, through a different procedural door.

Transforming the IDC from Grievance Body to Censorship Apparatus

The original Rule 14(2) required the IDC to hear "complaints regarding violation or contravention of the Code of Ethics." The amended version removes this requirement entirely. 

The IDC now hears:
(a) grievances arising from decisions at Level I or II; or
(b) "matters" referred to by the Ministry.

Clause (b) is unconstrained since, (a) there is no requirement that the "matter" arise from a complaint, (b) no requirement that the "matter" relate to a Code of Ethics violation; and (c) no requirement that the affected party be heard before the referral. The Ministry of Information and Broadcasting can, on its own motion, refer any content-related "matter" to the IDC. 

The cumulative effect of the amendments to Rules 8 and 14 is to reconstruct the oversight machinery that the Bombay and Madras High Courts found constitutionally suspect, in a form designed to evade the existing interim orders. The IDC, previously limited to the three-tier complaints process under the stayed Rules 9(3), 12, and 13 framework, now operates as a free-standing censorship committee that can take up "matters" referred by the executive.

Increased user surveillance through mandatory data retention directions

Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law. For instance, the mandatory data retention of user data beyond 180 days within Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h) may be prescribed for longer periods and other purposes raising risks of surveillance and even potentially data leaks of sensitive data that is stored for longer periods of time. Government mandates for data retention as to their legal authority and hence period of retention will be beyond those contained under the IT Act.

SOS for Digital Rights 

IFF urges an urgent rollback!

We are alarmed by the continuing expansion of unchecked executive power that is opposed to the Constitution of India. The present actions of MEITY smack of digital authoritarianism and we call on them to withdraw these proposed amendments. 

The proper course is to await judicial determination of the pending challenges, respect interim protections granted by constitutional courts, and pursue regulatory objectives through parliamentary legislation rather than subordinate instruments that exceed the parent statute.

If not withdrawn, IFF will file a detailed response before the comment deadline. We call upon all stakeholders to submit their objections before 14 April 2026 at itrules.consultation@meity.gov.in

Binance plans a UK comeback as a new crypto licence regime opens

What this means
Binance is preparing to apply to the Financial Conduct Authority for a cryptoasset licence when applications open next month. Basically, it's trying to get back into Britain ahead of a stricter rulebook that kicks in October 2027.

Hidden points
- The new rules will require a UK presence, enough financial and operational resources, and senior managers who pass "fit and proper" tests
- Binance is expected to set up a UK-based board as part of the application
- The FCA ordered Binance's UK entity to stop in 2021, then blocked promotions through a local partner in 2023
- Binance also paid $4.3 billion in 2023 to settle US AML and sanctions charges, and recently said it would restrict some EU customers after missing a MiCA licence

Real impact / takeaways
Here's the thing: this is a licence application, not a green light. Binance has already been thrown out of the UK twice in different ways — first the 2021 stop order, then the 2023 marketing clampdown. The kicker is timing: it wants to file as the window opens, before serving Brits from offshore gets a lot harder.

Investor / trader take
Binance is the name on the filing, but the trade is UK-and-EU regulatory access. A real FCA licence would reopen a market it's been locked out of; a rejection would fit the 2021/2023 pattern. Layer in the failed MiCA licence and the old US settlement, and this is a compliance-credibility test, not a growth announcement.

Bottom line
Binance is lining up an FCA cryptoasset-licence bid as Britain's new October 2027 rulebook approaches, after years of being blocked from the UK market.

THREAD 🧵 | Why the Supreme Court’s order regarding Imran Khan’s medical treatment can be defended through existing Pakistani precedents

If the Government files a Review Petition, Imran Khan’s legal team can rely on the following precedents. Not every case is identical, but together they establish important principles concerning medical bail, prisoners’ constitutional rights, State duty of care and judicial protection.

1/10 — Muhammad Yousafullah Khan v. The State — PLD 1995 SC 58
The Supreme Court recognized medical grounds as a basis for bail where the required treatment cannot adequately be provided in custody and continued detention may seriously affect the prisoner’s health.
This is one of the key authorities for the medical-bail test.

2/10 — Muhammad Saeed Mehdi v. The State — 2002 SCMR 282
Bench: Justice Muhammad Bashir Jehangiri, Justice Rana Bhagwandas & Justice Munir A. Sheikh.
The Supreme Court granted bail where the accused required immediate treatment, hospitalization and close monitoring by specialists in a properly equipped hospital.
The Court held that such treatment could not be achieved simply by keeping the person in custody and sending him to hospital only for limited treatment.
This is highly relevant to the argument that specialist treatment must actually be available, not merely theoretically accessible.

3/10 — Peer Mukaram-ul-Haq v. NAB — 2006 SCMR 1225
Bench: Justice Javed Iqbal & Justice Abdul Hameed Dogar.
The Supreme Court considered medical evidence showing that the required specialists and facilities were not available in the local hospital and granted bail.
The judgment is important because the Court looked at the actual availability of specialised medical facilities, rather than merely accepting that some basic treatment existed.

4/10 — Nawaz Sharif — Al-Azizia medical-bail case, March 2019
The Islamabad High Court had rejected medical relief, but the Supreme Court intervened and granted Nawaz Sharif six weeks’ bail on medical grounds and suspended his sentence.
Bench:
Chief Justice Asif Saeed Khan Khosa
Justice Sajjad Ali Shah
Justice Yahya Afridi
This precedent is particularly important because it demonstrates that the Supreme Court can independently examine medical evidence and grant appropriate relief even after a High Court has refused it.

5/10 — Mst. Safia Bano v. Home Department — PLD 2021 SC 488
The Supreme Court dealt extensively with mentally ill prisoners, medical assessment, Medical Boards, treatment and the humane administration of punishment.
The case supports the broader constitutional principle that imprisonment does not erase a prisoner’s fundamental rights or the State’s responsibility toward the prisoner’s health and humane treatment.

6/10 — Raja Azmat Ali v. Abu Malik Naseem — 2023 SCMR 1867
Bench: Chief Justice Umar Ata Bandial & Justice Athar Minallah.
This is one of the strongest prisoner-rights precedents.
The Supreme Court held that a prisoner — whether convicted or under trial — remains entitled to constitutional protection of life, dignity and fair treatment.
The Court emphasized that incarceration curtails liberty and freedom of movement, but does not extinguish fundamental rights. Because prisoners depend upon the State for protection of life, health and humane treatment, the State owes them a duty of care.
This is directly relevant to defending constitutional protection for Imran Khan.

#Constitution #ImranKhan #SupremeCourt #RuleOfLaw

7/10 — Shehla Zia v. WAPDA — PLD 1994 SC 693
Bench:
Chief Justice Nasim Hasan Shah
Justice Saleem Akhtar
Justice Manzoor Hussain Sial
The Supreme Court gave Article 9’s Right to Life a broad constitutional interpretation.
Although this was not a prisoner case, it provides an important constitutional foundation for arguments concerning protection of life, health and human safety.

8/10 — Muhammad Hussain v. The State — Peshawar High Court, https://t.co/1EKMQS3eG3 No. 3743-P/2020
The Peshawar High Court applied the established medical-bail principles where serious illness, the need for specialised treatment and the availability of adequate treatment in custody were relevant considerations.
This is particularly relevant because it is a High Court authority applying the medical-bail test in practice.

9/10 — Khawar Kayani v. The State — PLD 2022 SC 551
Crl.P. No. 345/2022 — Supreme Court of Pakistan
This case concerns statutory bail and the interpretation of the Juvenile Justice System Act rather than medical treatment.
It should therefore not be presented as a direct medical-bail precedent. Its value is in the broader principle that statutory provisions governing custody and bail must be interpreted according to the protective purpose of the law.

10/10 — Tahira Batool v. The State — PLD 2022 SC 764
Crl.P. No. 910/2022 — Supreme Court of Pakistan
The Supreme Court discussed the scope of the first proviso to Section 497(1) Cr.P.C. and emphasized that statutory exceptions to the normal bail framework must be properly considered.
Again, this is not a direct medical-transfer case, but it can be relevant when lawyers argue that statutory bail provisions should be interpreted according to their protective purpose.

CONCLUSION

The Legal Argument for Imran Khan
Taken together, these authorities provide several important lines of argument:
• Medical evidence matters.
• A prisoner does not lose constitutional rights merely because he is incarcerated.
• The State owes prisoners a duty of care regarding life, health and humane treatment.
• Where specialised treatment is required, the question is whether that treatment is actually available, not merely whether a basic prison medical facility exists.
• The Supreme Court has previously intervened on medical grounds even after a High Court refused relief.
• Prison Rules provide an administrative mechanism, but they cannot automatically extinguish constitutional protections under Articles 9 and 14.
The strongest authorities for the present issue are:
Nawaz Sharif (2019) — medical relief after IHC refusal
Muhammad Saeed Mehdi (2002 SCMR 282) — specialist hospital treatment
Peer Mukaram-ul-Haq (2006 SCMR 1225) — availability of specialised facilities
Safia Bano (PLD 2021 SC 488) — Medical Boards and prisoner health
Raja Azmat Ali (2023 SCMR 1867) — prisoner’s life, dignity and State duty of care
Shehla Zia (PLD 1994 SC 693) — constitutional protection of life
Therefore, the Government cannot simply argue:
“Prison Rules give the executive authority, therefore the Supreme Court had no power to intervene.”
The real question is whether the constitutional jurisdiction of the Court can be exercised where a prisoner’s life, health and dignity are at stake.
The above jurisprudence provides a substantial legal basis for arguing that it can.
The law must apply equally to every prisoner — including Imran Khan.

If Kamala Wins Again: What Actually Happens to America
Let’s stop pretending.
If Kamala Harris runs in 2028 and somehow wins, it will not be a “fresh start.” It will be a deliberate return to the same failed playbook that voters already rejected in 2024  only this time with fewer restraints and more institutional capture.
Here is the unvarnished reality of what that presidency looks like.
The border goes back to chaos.
As Vice President, Harris was tasked with the root causes of migration. The result was record illegal crossings, fentanyl flooding communities, and cities overwhelmed. She never visited the border in any meaningful capacity until political pressure forced optics. A second Harris administration would almost certainly restore the catch-and-release incentives, expand parole programs, and treat enforcement as the real problem. Expect another surge. Expect more strain on schools, hospitals, and housing in already struggling cities. This is not speculation  it is the documented pattern of the last administration she served in.
Energy and costs climb again.
Harris spent years signaling hostility to domestic oil and gas. She once said she wanted to ban fracking. The Biden-Harris years delivered higher energy prices and inflation that hit working families hardest. A Harris White House would double down on aggressive green mandates, slower permitting, and higher regulatory costs. The result is predictable: more expensive fuel, higher utility bills, and reduced American energy independence at the exact moment the world is unstable.
Taxes and spending expand.
Her 2024 platform leaned into higher corporate rates, higher capital gains taxes, and expanded credits paid for by “the rich.” The math never added up then, and it will not add up later. Combined with continued deficit spending, the pressure lands on the middle class through inflation and higher interest rates. The people who already paid the price once will pay it again.
Crime and soft-on-crime ideology return.
Harris’s record as California Attorney General and San Francisco District Attorney was defined by progressive prosecutors’ priorities: reduced cash bail experiments, reluctance to charge certain offenses, and a focus on “root causes” over accountability. Cities that followed that model saw measurable increases in property crime and disorder. A national version of that philosophy would slow the hard-won gains made under tougher enforcement.
Institutions get further politicized.
Harris has already floated revisiting the Electoral College and expanding the Supreme Court. That is not abstract theory. It is a direct response to losing under the current rules. Court packing, statehood for D.C. and Puerto Rico, and further erosion of Senate norms are not fringe ideas on the left they are recurring talking points when Democrats lose power. Expect them to move from rhetoric to active legislative pressure.
The culture war intensifies.
Identity, equity mandates, and speech restrictions would return with institutional force. Schools, corporations, and federal agencies would face renewed pressure to prioritize ideology over competence and results. Parents who already pushed back against this in 2021–2024 would find themselves fighting the same battles under a friendlier White House.
None of this is about her being the first woman or the first Black and South Asian vice president. Competence is not measured by identity checkboxes. It is measured by outcomes. The outcomes under the Biden-Harris years  inflation, border failure, urban disorder, and a public that felt ignored  were rejected at the ballot box.
A Harris victory in 2028 would not represent progress. It would represent a refusal to learn.
America already tried this. Voters already delivered the verdict. The only question left is whether enough people are willing to pretend the results were different the second time.
They will not be.

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2's Statement Against Arbitrary Takedown of Online Content

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 strongly objects to the arbitrary, unconstitutional takedown of online content deemed “objectionable, abusive, and offensive” by the Delhi Police today.

As reported, the Delhi Police's social media monitoring team has been scanning online platforms to identify objectionable content, and upon identification, has been sending notices to social media intermediaries directing them to remove the content. Both existing and newly uploaded content are being monitored, and at least three social media platforms have been served notices to take down content, subsequent to which, several posts have already been taken down.

This takedown drive is contrary to the rule of law and to India’s constitutional commitment to freedom of speech under Article 19(1)(a). The restrictions on free speech laid out in Article 19(2) are specific, and do not include “objectionable, abusive, or offensive” speech as one of the legitimate grounds to block free speech. Taking down content on the vague grounds that it is “objectionable” also directly contradicts the judgment of Shreya Singhal v Union of India, which struck down Section 66A of the Information Technology Act, 2000 precisely because the usage of words like “grossly offensive” and “menacing character” were undefined and therefore vague, arbitrary and unreasonable.

The current practice of issuing vague orders that invoke generic grounds such as “objectionable” or “offensive” is inconsistent with the safeguards laid down in Shreya Singhal. The Supreme Court upheld Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000 strictly because it required that blocking orders must be reasoned, necessary, and proportionate, and that such reasons must be recorded in writing to enable judicial review. In the present case, notices sent to social media intermediaries through the Sahyog Portal under Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act and Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules, 2021, leave users in the dark, with no recourse to meaningfully challenge takedowns and leave affected parties without legal redressal. The Sahyog Portal puts in place a parallel system to take down content online, without any of the safeguards present under Section 69A.

The opacity surrounding these takedowns goes against the strict requirements of accountability and record-keeping embedded in the Information Technology (Procedure and Safeguards for Blocking for Access of Information by Public) Rules, 2009. Instead, what we see emerging through these takedowns is a system of informal, decentralised censorship, where the government can direct content removals without transparency or oversight.

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 has consistently emphasised the need for transparency and primacy of user rights in content moderation. The cumulative effect of current developments is the creation of a black-box censorship regime, where users are silenced without any transparency or accessible remedies.

In light of the above, https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 calls for the following:

1. Immediate disclosure of all takedown orders issued to platforms, including specific reasons and legal justifications.

2. Strict adherence to the procedural safeguards laid out under Section 69A and the 2009 Blocking Rules, which were upheld by the Supreme Court in Shreya Singhal.

3. Notices received by social media intermediaries to be sent to every user affected to ensure transparency.

4. Strengthening of independent oversight and appellate mechanisms to ensure that users can effectively challenge unlawful restrictions.

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2’s statement on the Delhi Police notice directing X to remove content from the platform.

According to media reports, the Intelligence Fusion and Strategic Operations (“IFSO”) unit of the Delhi Police Special Cell has issued several notices to X, citing the IT (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 (“IT Rules 2021”), following complaints filed with the Delhi Police alleging circulation of “derogatory, malicious and defamatory content” targeting constitutional heads, particularly the Prime Minister, on the social media platform. The IFSO has also registered an F.I.R. under Sections 351(3), 353(2) and 356(2) of the Bharatiya Nyay Sanhita 2023, against several social media handles for posting such content.

In its “Intimation to Intermediary for Disabling Access to Unlawful Information” notices issued to X,  purportedly under provisions of IT Rules 2021, the IFSO directed the platform to:

- Delete/remove the alleged post/video from the platform immediately.

- Provide the complete registrant details including full name, address, contact details and email ID, of the X account ID holder who posted such content, as well as the login and logout details of the said account, along with corresponding time and date stamp, or any other details relevant for investigation.

 - To preserve information/ records relating to the said posts for future investigation, and furnish a certificate u/s  63(4) of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, in respect thereof.

This is not the first instance of large-scale removal of posts, as even earlier on 27 July 2026, Delhi Police reportedly instructed multiple social media intermediaries to take down posts/videos uploaded during the Jantar Mantar Protests that allegedly contained offensive or abusive remarks against the Prime Minister. Moreover, the Delhi Police’s social media monitoring team has been specifically engaged in monitoring online platforms for such content, and upon identifying objectionable posts, notices are issued to the concerned intermediaries directing them to remove the identified content.

At the outset, the legislative scheme of the IT Act 2000, does not contemplate/ permit the authorisation of the Delhi Police to direct the takedown of online content from social media platforms.

The power to block public access to online information or content is exclusively traceable to Section 69A of the IT Act 2000, which vests such power solely in the Central Government, or an officer specially authorised by it.  Whereas, Section 79(3)(b) of IT Act merely grants safe harbour to intermediaries, subject to compliance with due diligence obligations. In no circumstance can Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act 2000 or IT Rules 2021 confer a power upon the Central or State Government to devise a mechanism or appoint any agency/ officer for regulating or restricting free speech online. Reliance is placed on Shreya Singhal v. Union of India, (2015) 5 SCC 1 (para 121).

Notably, the IT (Blocking) Rules 2009 already outline procedure and rules for the designation of an officer, not below the rank of Joint Secretary, empowered to issue directions under Section 69A for blocking public access to online information. However, neither Section 69A nor the IT (Blocking) Rules, 2009 authorise the Central Government, or any State executive, to constitute a Nodal Agency empowered to direct the blocking of public access to online content.

Despite the above legislative scheme, on 26 December 2024, the Lieutenant Governor of the NCT of Delhi, purportedly in exercise of powers under the first proviso to Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT  Rules 2021 read with Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act 2000, issued a Notification appointing the Delhi Police as the Nodal Agency and Deputy Commissioners of Police (of various divisions) as designated officers for issuing takedown notices. Consequently, the Delhi Police has been issuing takedown notices pursuant to the said Notification.  However, this Notification, being founded upon a provision and subordinate legislation that do not authorise the creation of such a mechanism, is ex facie illegal and ultra vires the IT Act 2000. The legality of the said Notification has been challenged by https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 in a Petition before the Delhi High Court on the aforesaid ground, among others. The Petition is registered as W.P.(C) 7650/2025, titled “Software Freedom Law Center, India v. State of NCT of Delhi & Ors.”

Without prejudice to the aforesaid, both Section 69A and Section 79(3)(b) read with IT Rules 2021, outline overbroad grounds. While Section 69A empowers the Central Government to issue notice for blocking public access to online information on overbroad grounds such as "public order"; Section 79(3)(b) read with the IT Rules 2021 outline expansive grounds such as content’s use in the commission of an unlawful act relating to public order, decency or morality, defamation, etc., or where such information is prohibited under any prevailing law.  Since these grounds are decided by an executive order, without any judicial determination, their overbroad nature renders them susceptible to misuse and overreach. Therefore, even mere profanity, satire, or genuine criticism may be directed to be removed pursuant to such orders. This leaves the fundamental right to freedom of speech and expression vulnerable.

The risk of misuse and overreach is further exacerbated by the compliance regime applicable to intermediaries. An intermediary is likely to err on the side of over-compliance rather than independently assess the legality of a removal request, owing to the extremely limited timeline for compliance and the severe consequences of non-compliance. Under Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act read with Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules 2021, an intermediary is required to comply with a removal order within three hours, leaving virtually no scope for any meaningful independent assessment to guard against misuse or excessive application of such powers. Further, failure to comply exposes the intermediary to the risk of imprisonment for up to 7 years and fine for requests issued u.s. 69 A [Section 69A(3)], or the loss of safe harbour protection for orders issued u.s. 79(3)(b) [Section 79].

Moreover, when mere profanity expressed in anger against a governmental policy, or as part of political criticism, becomes the subject of penal investigation, it seriously undermines the fundamental right to freedom of speech and expression. We condemn any penal action in such circumstances, as it creates a significant chilling effect on the exercise of free speech by citizens, who are entitled to express their disagreement, dissatisfaction, or anger towards governmental policies through peaceful expression and dialogue.

To safeguard the online freedom of speech of these users, https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2’s RightsLine provides free legal assistance and support to anyone facing content takedowns or account suspensions. Our team can help individuals understand their options and navigate the available redress mechanisms. 

Report at https://t.co/jzMiSxaaBB or mail us at rightsline@sflc.in

April 4, 2026 | New Delhi: The Editors Guild of India is deeply concerned by both the contents and the underlying intent behind the Draft Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Second Amendment Rules, 2026 (“Draft Amendments”), which were made public by the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) on March 30, 2026, with just a fortnight given for comments.
Prima facie, the amended rules and guidelines, whose stated purpose is to “strengthen compliance” and increase the effectiveness of regulatory oversight of content regulation mechanisms under Part III (Code of Ethics relating to Digital Media) of the IT Rules, 2021” appear to arm MeitY with sweeping powers of content regulation, sharply increases the compliance burden on digital intermediaries, and gives the executive overarching powers to block or take down content generated by  “non news publishers” and intermediaries. This will directly infringe the fundamental right to free speech guaranteed to all citizens under the Constitution and will have a chilling effect on freedom of expression and the airing of contrarian views, which are fundamental to an open and functional democracy.
Sub-rule (4) to Rule 3, which deals with due diligence obligations of intermediaries, now makes it mandatory on the part of intermediaries to comply with “any clarification, advisory, order, direction, standard operating procedure, code of practice or guideline issued by the ministry, by order in writing”. Failure to comply has been linked to loss of the safe harbour protection extended to intermediaries and platforms for user-generated content, under section 79 of the Information Technology Act. The absence of due process for the issuance of compliance orders and the complete lack of transparency in the process are deeply concerning.
Changes to Rule 14(2) and Rule 14(5) in the draft amendment also greatly widen the powers of the Inter-Departmental Committee (IDC). IDC, a central oversight body constituted under Rule 14 of the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021, was specifically created to hear grievances and complaints against digital content. Now, the IDC has been empowered to deal with and “matter” – a generalisation which arms the body to consider virtually any issue, in the absence of any definition of what constitutes a “matter”. Other provisions devolve rulemaking powers entirely to the executive branch, removing the window for legislative oversight provided under the IT Act.
The EGi calls on the government to urgently review or recall the draft rules, and engage in more constructive consultations with all sections of stakeholders and take on board valid concerns and objections.
Warm regards,
Sanjay Kapoor, President
Raghavan Srinivasan, General Secretary
Teresa Rehman, Treasurer

Prof. Manoj Kumar Jha @manojkjhadu, your “Muffled Voices” poses a question India cannot afford to answer casually: what if democracy survives electorally, yet citizens gradually become afraid to speak? 

More unsettling still—what if nobody formally silences us because anticipated consequences teach us to silence ourselves?

🧵 FREEDOM OF EXPRESSION & DEMOCRACY’S FATE: THE CONSTITUTIONAL ANATOMY OF A “CHILLING EFFECT”

You begin where democracy actually begins—not with elections, but information.

Alexander Meiklejohn's democratic theory treated speech as indispensable to self-government: citizens cannot meaningfully govern unless they can hear, question and judge competing claims.

India constitutionalises that intuition through Article 19(1)(a).

But freedom is deliberately not absolute. Article 19(2) permits reasonable restrictions concerning sovereignty and integrity of India, State security, friendly relations with foreign States, public order, decency or morality, contempt of court, defamation and incitement to an offence.

The constitutional equation is therefore neither:

Speech > everything

nor

State > speech

but:

Liberty + narrowly justified restraint = constitutional democracy.

The Supreme Court has repeatedly stressed that restrictions cannot simply be invented beyond Article 19(2)'s enumerated grounds.

text:
India already possesses a constitutional compass.

Romesh Thappar (1950) located circulation of ideas near democracy's foundations.

Bennett Coleman (1972) protected press freedom against measures whose practical effect constrained circulation.

Indian Express Newspapers (1985) reaffirmed press freedom within Article 19(1)(a).

Shreya Singhal (2015) struck down IT Act Section 66A, powerfully distinguishing discussion, advocacy and incitement.

Subramanian Swamy (2016) nevertheless upheld criminal defamation—reminding absolutists that reputation also receives constitutional protection.

Anuradha Bhasin (2020) reaffirmed press freedom and subjected restrictions affecting internet-based expression to constitutional scrutiny, while discussing chilling effect.

The jurisprudential message is beautifully difficult:

Protect dissent without constitutionalising abuse; regulate harm without bureaucratising truth.

Your @manojkjhadu concern over governmental “fact-checking” acquires special contemporary significance.

The Bombay High Court struck down the 2023 IT Rules amendment enabling a Central Government Fact Check Unit concerning information about Central Government business, finding constitutional defects including vagueness and restrictions beyond Article 19(2).

But the story is not finished.

As of 20 August 2026, the Union's appeal is alive before the Supreme Court. 

In March 2026, the Court issued notice, declined to stay the Bombay High Court judgment and indicated that significant constitutional questions concerning misinformation require consideration.

That makes Jha's question remarkably current:

Can Government legitimately combat misinformation concerning itself without becoming simultaneously interested party, complainant and arbiter of truth?

Equally:

Can constitutional democracy simply abandon the information ecosystem to commercially incentivised misinformation?

Neither extreme solves the problem.

Independent process, statutory precision, transparency, proportionality and judicial review offer the more defensible middle path.

Bad becomes worse? Further changes proposed to the proposed changes to IT Rules!

Today, post-noon on 21 April 2026, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) has published further proposed amendments to the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Second Amendment Rules, 2026.

The notice states that these are limited to Rule 3(3)(a)(ii) requiring that labels identifying synthetically generated information be continuously and clearly visible throughout the duration of the content in visual display. This goes beyond the earlier requirement of “prominent” visibility, and now mandates persistent, uninterrupted disclosure for the entire duration of such content. This requirement is applicable to all users of social media and AI tools, and not just digital news platforms.

All other provisions in the newly updated draft remain the same as the draft circulated on 30 March 2026. Our comments to the MeitY are available here. The consultation timeline has now been extended allowing stakeholders to submit comments on both the earlier draft amendments and these additional amendments by 07 May 2026. We note that suggesting changes within the window of a pre-existing public consultation process in which thousands of Indians have voiced opposition is likely to result in, “consultation fatigue” and at the very least demonstrates a pattern of ad-hoc policy making than one which accounts for structured and planned feedback.

Further, MeitY has once again indicated that the submissions will be held in fiduciary capacity in MeitY and shall not be disclosed to any one at any stage, enabling persons to submit feedback/comments freely without any hesitation. Importantly, consultation processes are important for democratic decision making, placing the responses in the public domain would ensure meaningful engagement and participation by stakeholders. It would also allow for better analysis, understanding, and fair critique of the various perspectives put forward. We therefore urge MeitY to place the comments and feedback on their website in the interest of democracy and transparency.

We urge citizenry to participate in such public consultation and share their feedback/comments on the draft rules in a rule wise manner by email to itrules.consultation@meity.gov.in in MS Word or PDF format by 07th May, 2026. We have drafted a short template email which readers can improvise upon.

As of today, more than 4500 people have used our link to improve upon and send their own comments to MeitY primarily asking for a withdrawal of the proposed changes to the IT Rules, 2021.

Sound the Alarm : IFF’s First Read on MeitY's Draft IT Rules Second Amendment, 2026

New Delhi, 30 March 2026

On 30 March 2026, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology published proposed amendments to the IT Rules, 2021, inviting public comments by 14 April,  a comment period of barely fifteen days for changes with far reaching consequences for free speech and intermediary governance in India. We have conducted a quick review of the draft amendments. Despite being presented as "clarificatory and procedural," they represent a dangerous expansion of executive power over online speech.

We wish to state at the outset that these proposed amendments need to be immediately withdrawn and every member in our citizenry should demand their roll back and stand with the Constitution of India. These proposed amendments come at a time of fear and increased government directed censorship, especially of online political speech that includes parody and satire of the government, including the Prime Minister.

In brief the five changes are listed below:

1. Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h): Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law.

2. Rule 3(4): Insertion of a new clause that mandates intermediary compliance with MeitY-issued clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines, making such compliance a condition for retaining safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act. These are not anchored to the rule making powers of the IT Act, 2000 and provide uncanalised power to MEITY despite it stating otherwise.

3. Rule 8(1) proviso: A substitution in the proviso that expands applicability of MIB’s oversight mechanism in Part III of the rules to:  (1) intermediaries and (2) users who are not “publishers” and post/share news and current affairs content online. This oversight mechanism contains the blocking powers of MIB by way of Rule 14 (Inter-Departmental Committee), Rule 15 (Procedure for issuing directions to block), and Rule 16 (Emergency blocking provisions).

4. Rule 14(2) : A substitution that expands the scope of the IDC from hearing "complaints or grievances" to hearing "matters", including those referred by the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting.

5. Rule 14(5) : Replaces "complaints or grievances" with "the matter" in relation to IDC examination and recommendations.

A massive expansion of an unconstitutional censorship and regulatory power

First and most concerningly, Rule 3(4) creates a sweeping power for MeitY to issue binding instruments which are not anchored in law such as clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines that intermediaries must comply with as a condition of safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act.

The Supreme Court's 2015 judgment in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, remains the foundational precedent governing intermediary liability. It constrains the proposed amendments in several ways. First, the court read down Section 79(3)(b) to require that "actual knowledge" of unlawful content must come through a court order or government notification. Any Rule 3(4) making MeitY, "clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs", lower the constitutional threshold for intermediary due diligence obligations.

Further, the settled principle in Indian administrative law, reaffirmed in Indian Express Newspapers v. Union of India (1985) 1 SCC 641 and Confederation of Ex-Servicemen Associations v. Union of India (2006) 8 SCC 399, is that delegated legislation must remain within the four corners of the parent statute.  It is important to note that the rule-making power under Section 87(1) of the IT Act is confined to, "carry[ing] out the provisions" of the Act. Section 87(2)(zg) authorizes rules for intermediary guidelines under Section 79(2), and Section 87(2)(z) for blocking procedures under Section 69A(2). Justice Chandurkar's judgement in the Kunal Kamra case clearly found the FCU amendment was not properly referable to either provision. Hence, any Rule 3(4) mandating compliance with MeitY advisories would face identical challenges since they create substantive new obligations not contemplated by Sections 79 or 87.

Even though Rule 3(4)(b)(ii) states that such, “advisories” etc. need to, “clearly specify the statutory provision or legal basis under which it is issued”, since these are not required to be published or made public there is every likelihood these will be issued with secrecy and hence may just in a tautological manner refer back to Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act. This is similar to a logical fallacy in which it is clearly observable that a student is cheating on an exam who then claims that they may be permitted to continue cheating since they are stating at the same time they are not cheating. 

The practical effect of Rule 3(4) is that intermediaries face a perpetual compliance threat. Any failure to comply with any MeitY-issued instrument, however vague, however rapidly issued may cost them their safe harbour. The response for an intermediary is over-compliance and over-censorship.

Circumventing existing stay orders

The original proviso to Rule 8(1) stated that Part III applied to intermediaries only "for the purposes of rules 15 and 16"  i.e., content blocking directions and emergency blocking. The amended proviso now extends this to Rule 14, bringing intermediaries and user-generated news/current affairs content under the jurisdiction of the Inter-Departmental Committee.

Under Rules 9(1) and 9(3) of the 2021 IT Rules, there is a Code of Ethics compliance requirement and the three-tier grievance redressal mechanism, both of which were stayed by the Bombay High Court on 14 August 2021 as prima facie violative of Article 19(1)(a) and ultra vires the IT Act. On the oversight mechanism in Rules 14, 15, and 16, the Bombay High Court granted the petitioners to seek relief on this rule when an Inter Departmental Committee is established. The Madras High Court affirmed this stay as having pan-India effect in its order of 16 September 2021 in T.M. Krishna v. Union of India, observing that "an oversight mechanism to control the media by the government may rob the media of its independence." 

Both these cases, along with other cases challenging various provisions of the 2021 IT Rules, are now pending adjudication before the Delhi High Court.

The expansion of Rule 8(1) to cover Rules 14, 15, and 16 is an attempt to expand the blocking powers of MIB to both intermediaries and users who are not “publishers” but post news and current affairs content online. The IDC can now examine "matters" relating to user-generated news content on intermediary platforms without the Code of Ethics framework having been adjudicated as constitutional; the government effectively obtains the content oversight machinery that three High Courts found illegal, through a different procedural door.

Transforming the IDC from Grievance Body to Censorship Apparatus

The original Rule 14(2) required the IDC to hear "complaints regarding violation or contravention of the Code of Ethics." The amended version removes this requirement entirely. 

The IDC now hears:
(a) grievances arising from decisions at Level I or II; or
(b) "matters" referred to by the Ministry.

Clause (b) is unconstrained since, (a) there is no requirement that the "matter" arise from a complaint, (b) no requirement that the "matter" relate to a Code of Ethics violation; and (c) no requirement that the affected party be heard before the referral. The Ministry of Information and Broadcasting can, on its own motion, refer any content-related "matter" to the IDC. 

The cumulative effect of the amendments to Rules 8 and 14 is to reconstruct the oversight machinery that the Bombay and Madras High Courts found constitutionally suspect, in a form designed to evade the existing interim orders. The IDC, previously limited to the three-tier complaints process under the stayed Rules 9(3), 12, and 13 framework, now operates as a free-standing censorship committee that can take up "matters" referred by the executive.

Increased user surveillance through mandatory data retention directions

Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law. For instance, the mandatory data retention of user data beyond 180 days within Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h) may be prescribed for longer periods and other purposes raising risks of surveillance and even potentially data leaks of sensitive data that is stored for longer periods of time. Government mandates for data retention as to their legal authority and hence period of retention will be beyond those contained under the IT Act.

SOS for Digital Rights 

IFF urges an urgent rollback!

We are alarmed by the continuing expansion of unchecked executive power that is opposed to the Constitution of India. The present actions of MEITY smack of digital authoritarianism and we call on them to withdraw these proposed amendments. 

The proper course is to await judicial determination of the pending challenges, respect interim protections granted by constitutional courts, and pursue regulatory objectives through parliamentary legislation rather than subordinate instruments that exceed the parent statute.

If not withdrawn, IFF will file a detailed response before the comment deadline. We call upon all stakeholders to submit their objections before 14 April 2026 at itrules.consultation@meity.gov.in

DigiLocker is safer than a plastic folder — unless you download the fake app

On 29 November 2025, the official Digital India handle posted a warning that should have been louder than it was. Fraudulent apps with names like DigiLocker were circulating on app stores. The instruction was blunt: use only the authentic DigiLocker application. If you had already installed a suspicious version, delete it and change the passwords on linked accounts.

Moneycontrol reported the advisory the next day. Times of India followed for students. This is the incident. I am not going to invent a victim. The government warning is the case.

Why a plastic folder loses

A plastic folder can be stolen, soaked, or left on a bus. DigiLocker is safer than that folder for a simple reason. It is not a photo album of papers you scanned. It is a wallet that government issuers can push documents into.

The official site is https://t.co/kNUXgk5XJe. From there you can access, share, and get government-issued documents verified: a driving licence, a vehicle RC, marksheets, and other records the issuer has actually placed in your account.

How it works, without the brochure language

You open an account that is authenticated with Aadhaar. Then an RTO, a school board, a university, or another issuer sends a digitally signed document into that account. When a verifier checks it, they are not squinting at a JPEG you uploaded. They are looking at the issuer's signature.

That is why a screenshot is not the same thing. A screenshot is a picture. An issued DigiLocker document is a signed record from the source. You can crop a marksheet photo in two minutes. You cannot forge the issuer's signature by taking a better photo.

MeitY has been clear on the legal point. Issued documents in DigiLocker are deemed at par with originals. The official about page says the same thing under the IT Act, and in more formal language under Rule 9A of the 2016 Digital Locker rules. You can show a digital driving licence, or pull a Class X or Class XII marksheet, without laminating another photocopy.

That legal status is useful only if you are inside the real locker.

The live warning

A clone that looks like DigiLocker does not need to "hack the government." It only needs you to type an Aadhaar number and share an OTP. DigiLocker does not make you unhackable. The risk moved. Paper used to get lost. Now someone tries to phish the OTP that opens the locker.

The authentic app is published by the National e-Governance Division (NeGD), Government of India. The official website is https://t.co/kNUXgk5XJe. Install from there, or from the store listing that site points to. Confirm the developer name before you tap Install.

Do not install from a forwarded WhatsApp link. Do not trust a search ad that says "DigiLocker KYC" and asks for an OTP on a random page. No genuine officer needs that code from you on a link they just sent.

If a suspicious version is already on the phone, do what the advisory said. Delete it. Change the passwords on linked accounts. Then install the real app and check which documents are actually sitting there.

What to do before you need it

Before a road trip, open the real app and pull your driving licence and RC. Do it at home, on your own Wi-Fi, while you are not being rushed by a checkpoint or a rental desk.

Before admissions or a job file, students can pull marksheets from the board instead of hunting a laminated copy. If a verifier will accept DigiLocker, give them the issued document, not a crop of your screen.

Never share an OTP for "DigiLocker KYC" on a random link. The locker is tied to Aadhaar. The OTP is the key. Anyone who wants the key on a page you did not open from https://t.co/AE2sh860xw is not helping you file a document.

If you already downloaded something that only looked official, treat it as a live problem, not an embarrassing mistake. Delete the app. Change passwords. Watch bank and Aadhaar-linked SMS for a few days. Then start again from the official site.

The honest limit

A plastic folder fails when you lose it. DigiLocker fails when you hand the key to a lookalike. The folder is still worse for rain. The lookalike is worse for everything else.

Use the real locker. Pull the issued document, not a screenshot. Keep the OTP to yourself. That is the whole guide.

This article is written for general education and is not legal advice. It does not claim DigiLocker cannot be abused. The risk moved from lost paper to phishing for your Aadhaar OTP.

Sources: DigiLocker official site https://t.co/T2NXjM8lAm; DigiLocker About (issued documents at par with originals, IT Act / Rule 9A); MeitY statement that issued DigiLocker documents are deemed at par with originals; Digital India on X, 29 Nov 2025, authentic-app warning; Moneycontrol, 30 Nov 2025, fake DigiLocker apps advisory; Times of India Education, 11 Dec 2025, student guidance to use official sources.

India–US Relations Since 1947

India–US relations have evolved from Cold War-era differences and strategic distance into a broad-based strategic partnership covering defence, technology, trade, energy, space, critical minerals and the Indo-Pacific.

The Beginning: 1947–1962

India and the United States established diplomatic relations in 1946, even before India became independent.

After independence, India followed a policy of Non-Alignment, choosing not to formally join either the US-led or Soviet-led Cold War blocs.

The two countries nevertheless cooperated in:

• Economic and development assistance
• Food security and agriculture
• Education and scientific cooperation
• Economic and technical assistance

However, the United States developed close security ties with Pakistan, while India maintained increasingly close relations with the Soviet Union.

1962: India-China War
The 1962 India-China War created temporary strategic convergence.

The United States provided military assistance to India during the conflict, demonstrating that shared concerns over China could create space for cooperation.

The Difficult Phase: 1960s–1980s

Relations remained complicated because of Cold War geopolitics.

1971: India–Pakistan War

The 1971 India–Pakistan War became one of the lowest points in India–US relations. US supported Pakistan, while India had signed the Indo-Soviet Treaty of Peace, Friendship and Cooperation.

The episode reinforced India's perception of the US as being strategically aligned with Pakistan.

1974: India's First Nuclear Test

India conducted its first nuclear test at Pokhran in 1974. US strongly opposed India's nuclear programme, and nuclear proliferation became a major source of tension.

Overall Character of the Cold War Period

India–US relations were shaped by:

• India's Non-Alignment
• US–Pakistan relations
• India–Soviet relations
• Nuclear differences
• Different approaches to Cold War politics

The relationship was therefore marked by strategic distance despite shared democratic values.

The Turning Point: 1991–2000

The end of the Cold War fundamentally changed the relationship. India also introduced economic liberalisation in 1991, creating new opportunities for trade, investment and technology cooperation. The collapse of the Soviet Union reduced the geopolitical importance of the earlier India–US divide.

1998: Nuclear Tests
India conducted nuclear tests at Pokhran in May 1998. The United States imposed sanctions, but diplomatic engagement continued.

1999: Kargil War

The Kargil War became an important turning point. The United States pressured Pakistan to withdraw its forces from the Line of Control.This contributed to greater strategic understanding between India and the US.

2000: Clinton's Visit

US President Bill Clinton's visit to India in 2000 marked a major improvement in bilateral relations.The relationship increasingly shifted from Cold War differences towards economic and strategic engagement.

Strategic Partnership: 2000–2008

The early 21st century witnessed a major transformation.

2005: Civil Nuclear Deal

The India–US Civil Nuclear Agreement became a landmark breakthrough.

It enabled greater civilian nuclear cooperation with India despite India not being a member of the NPT. The agreement eventually contributed to the 2008 NSG waiver, allowing India to participate in international civilian nuclear commerce.

Why It Was Important

• Reduced India's nuclear isolation.
• Opened civilian nuclear cooperation.
• Increased strategic trust.
• Recognised India's growing global importance.
• Fundamentally changed the bilateral relationship.

Defence Partnership: 2010s

Defence cooperation expanded rapidly.

The two countries increased:

• Military exercises
• Defence trade
• Maritime security cooperation
• Intelligence sharing
• Defence technology cooperation

India was designated a Major Defense Partner by the United States in 2016.

Major Defence Agreements

• LEMOA – 2016 Logistics support and access between the armed forces.

• COMCASA – 2018 Secure communications and interoperability.

• BECA – 2020 Sharing of geospatial information and advanced military data.

These agreements strengthened military cooperation while supporting India's defence modernisation.

Indo-Pacific: A New Strategic Pillar

The rise of China and growing strategic competition in the Indo-Pacific have created greater convergence between India and the United States.

The two countries cooperate through the Quad, along with Japan and Australia.

Areas of cooperation include:

• Maritime security
• Freedom of navigation
• Supply-chain resilience
• Critical technologies
• Humanitarian assistance and disaster relief
• A free, open and inclusive Indo-Pacific
The Indo-Pacific has therefore become one of the central pillars of contemporary India–US relations.

Technology & Emerging Sectors
The relationship has expanded beyond traditional defence and diplomacy.

Critical & Emerging Technology cooperation includes:

• Artificial Intelligence
• Semiconductors
• Quantum technology
• Biotechnology
• Telecommunications
• Cybersecurity

The Initiative on Critical and Emerging Technology (iCET) has strengthened cooperation in these areas.

Space

India and the US cooperate in:

• Earth observation
• Satellite technology
• Space exploration
• Human spaceflight
• Space situational awareness

Critical Minerals

Both countries are working towards resilient supply chains for minerals essential for:

• Electric vehicles
• Batteries
• Renewable energy
• Semiconductors
• Defence technology

Economic Relationship

The United States is one of India's most important economic partners.
Major areas include:
• Trade and investment
• Information technology
• Pharmaceuticals
• Electronics
• Defence manufacturing
• Energy
• Digital economy
• Services

The Indian diaspora in the United States also acts as an important bridge between the two countries.
Current Situation: 2025–26

The return of Donald Trump to the US presidency in January 2025 has introduced a more transactional dimension to the relationship.

Strategic cooperation remains strong, but trade, tariffs and India's relationship with Russia have emerged as major areas of friction.

Strategic Cooperation Continues

Prime Minister Narendra Modi and President Donald Trump met in February 2025 and reaffirmed the importance of the bilateral relationship.

The two sides focused on:

• Defence cooperation
• Trade and investment
• Critical and emerging technologies
• Critical minerals
• Energy security
• Space cooperation
• Indo-Pacific security

Thus, despite disagreements, the strategic foundation of the relationship remains strong.

Trade & Tariffs :
Trade has become one of the major areas of tension.
The Trump administration has pushed for:
• Lower Indian tariffs
• Greater market access for US goods
• Reduction of trade barriers
• A more balanced trade relationship

India and the US have continued negotiations towards a broader bilateral trade agreement.

The key challenge is balancing:

US demand for greater market access with India's protection of domestic producers and strategic sectors.

Russia: A Major Test

India's continued defence and energy relationship with Russia remains a sensitive issue. The United States has sought to pressure countries to reduce dependence on Russian energy.
India, however, continues to emphasise:
• Energy security
• Strategic autonomy
• National interest
• Independent foreign-policy decision-making
This creates a difficult balancing act for India.

India wants stronger ties with US without compromising its long-standing relationship with Russia.

Defence: Strongest Area of Convergence

Defence remains one of the strongest pillars of India–US relations.
Cooperation includes:
• Defence procurement
• Military exercises
• Maritime security
• Intelligence and surveillance
• Defence technology
• Co-production
• Indo-Pacific security

The relationship is increasingly moving from buyer–seller relations towards technology sharing and defence co-production.

China & the Indo-Pacific

China remains an important factor behind India–US strategic convergence.

Both countries seek:

• A free and open Indo-Pacific
• Secure sea lanes
• Resilient supply chains
• Greater maritime cooperation
• Reduced dependence on vulnerable supply chains

However, India does not want its relationship with the United States to become a formal anti-China alliance.

India's approach remains:
Strategic cooperation + Strategic autonomy

Why India–US Relations Are Strategically Important ?

1. Indo-Pacific Security
The US is an important partner in India's effort to maintain a free, open, inclusive and rules-based Indo-Pacific.

2. Defence Modernisation
US defence technology and cooperation can strengthen India's military capabilities and domestic defence manufacturing.

3. China

Growing Chinese influence has created greater strategic convergence between India and the US.

4. Technology

Cooperation in AI, semiconductors, quantum technology and space can strengthen India's technological capabilities.

5. Economic Security

Both countries have an interest in diversified and resilient supply chains.

6. Global Governance

India and the US increasingly cooperate on global challenges while India seeks a greater role in institutions such as the UN Security Council and other multilateral platforms.

India's Approach: Partnership Without Alliance

India's relationship with the US reflects its broader foreign-policy principle of strategic autonomy.
India cooperates closely with US on:
• Defence
• Technology
• Indo-Pacific security
• Counter-terrorism
• Critical minerals

At the same time, India maintains important relations with:
• Russia
• European countries
• Japan
• ASEAN
• West Asian countries

This reflects India's approach of multi-alignment — cooperating with different powers according to national interests rather than becoming part of a fixed alliance bloc.

India–US relations have travelled a long distance since 1947 from Cold War-era strategic distance to a comprehensive strategic partnership.The relationship today covers defence, technology, trade, space, critical minerals, energy and Indo-Pacific security. At the same time, differences over tariffs, trade, Russia and energy policy demonstrate that the partnership is not an alliance.

For India, the objective is to cooperate with the United States where interests converge, manage differences where they exist, and preserve strategic autonomy.

States’ rights. States’ revenue. Stronger India.

The MMDR Amendment Act, 2026 brings greater clarity and stability to India’s mineral sector—while keeping States’ revenue and land rights protected. This reform is about creating a more predictable, transparent and future-ready mining ecosystem.

A report by The Indian Express has highlighted the sharp rise in government-issued blocking orders to social media platforms between March and July, during the period of the CJP student protests.

Most of these directions were issued through the Sahyog portal, a government platform used by Central and state agencies to send blocking notices to social media companies. The report says many of these orders were issued under Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act, 2000, which requires intermediaries to remove unlawful content to retain their legal protection. These are separate from blocking directions issued under Section 69A of the IT Act.

The report also says Meta has integrated its API with Sahyog to comply with the government’s 2–3-hour deadline, potentially allowing content flagged through government directions to be blocked automatically without a separate human review.

Digital-rights advocates have raised concerns about this mechanism and its implications for due process and freedom of expression.
